identity.name: Poland (Polish People's Republic and Third Polish Republic)

land.text: the pre-war Polish lands west of the Curzon Line that stayed Polish (Warsaw, Lublin, Kraków, Łódź, Poznań and the rest of central Poland), the overlap of the Second Polish Republic of 1939 and the shape of 1953

predecessors.note: Cliopatria's Second Polish Republic row ends in 1939 and nothing covers 1940-1952; the Polish Committee of National Liberation of summer 1944 became the Provisional Government of the Republic of Poland on 1 January 1945, which is the start taken here (the Provisional Government of National Unity followed in June 1945; the infobox gives 1947). The state's land comes from the occupier, nazi-germany, by the founding and the January and March gains, and from the Soviet Union and the Allied administration of Germany in August 1945; the Second Republic is the legal predecessor only. The Kresy east of the Curzon Line "which the Soviet Union had occupied in 1939" stayed with the USSR (border agreement of 16 August 1945). Other groups write the Second Republic and the wartime states.

capitals.name: Łódź
capitals.note: Infobox "Łódź (1947-1949) Warsaw (1949-1989)". The page does not give the seat for 1945-1946 (the Provisional Government of June 1945), so the years before 1947 are uncovered.

capitals.name: Warsaw
capitals.note: Infobox "Warsaw (1949-1989)"; "The capital and largest city is Warsaw" (Third Polish Republic page).

correction.text: The frontiers of 1953 held from 1945: the pre-war lands west of the Curzon Line plus "former German territory east of the Oder-Neisse line"; the 1951 exchange of land with the Ukrainian SSR is not applied because no opened page dates or sizes it

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria has no Polish shape for 1945-1952. Poland since 1945 "covers 312,677 km2" against 389,720 km2 for the Second Republic ("Poland lost 77,035 km2 compared to its pre-WWII territory", Polish People's Republic page). The 1953 shape (314,574 km2) is within 1 % of the 312,677 km2. The outline builds in 1945 (see the ledger): the General Government core on 1 January, Wartheland, the Katowice and Ciechanów districts in January, Danzig and Danzig-West Prussia in March, the five western voivodeships (Potsdam, 2 August) and the Białystok and Przemyśl areas (16 August) in August; the one-year step shows the 1953 outline from 1945 on, which covers all but 13 of its 1341 cells.

1953-1968, 314,574 km2: ratio 1.006 against 312,677 km2 (Territorial changes page), 312,685 km2 (infobox of the Polish People's Republic page, no year). The pages opened are silent on the 1951 exchange with the Soviet Union and on Czechoslovak border corrections, so no border change is dated inside the years of this shape.

1969-1989, 314,618 km2 (+44 km2, noise). The Treaty of Warsaw with West Germany followed in 1970 ("In 1970 West Germany signed treaties with the Soviet Union ... and Poland (Treaty of Warsaw)", adhered "with reservations, in 1972"): it recognised, did not move, the line. In 1989 "another treaty was signed between Poland and East Germany" defining the sea border.

1990-1991, 314,151 km2 (-467 km2, -0.15 %). The year matches the German-Polish Border Treaty signed 14 November 1990 ("finalizing the Oder-Neisse line as the German-Polish border") but the page describes no land changing hands; treated as a small sea-border or outline adjustment at confidence 2.

1992-2023, 314,108 km2 (-43 km2). The Border Treaty "came into force on 16 January 1992" (Oder-Neisse page) and Poland and Ukraine "confirmed the border on 18 May 1992" (Poland-Ukraine border page): the final settlement of the frontiers; no land is recorded as changing hands. Infobox of the Third Polish Republic page 312,696 km2 (no year), ratio 1.00.

region.text: the land the Warsaw government held at the start: the former General Government inside modern Poland (Warsaw, Lublin, Kraków, Radom, Kielce and the Vistula and San lands), that is the pre-war Polish land that was neither annexed to Germany in 1939 nor taken by the USSR in 1939; the Białystok and Przemyśl areas are left out (they return in 1945-08)

ledger.note: 1945: the Polish state of the Warsaw government begins. "On 1 January 1945, the committee was replaced by the Provisional Government of the Republic of Poland" (the Polish Committee of National Liberation, established "in the summer of 1944"); "The Provisional Government of National Unity was established in June 1945" (Polish People's Republic page): a reorganisation of the same state, not a new one. The page names no boundary: the region is the researcher's reading, the General Government land that nazi-germany gives up (its /ledger/68 region, trimmed to the 1953 outline), whose cities fell after 1 January (Warsaw "taken on 17 January", Kraków "secured undamaged on 19 January": Vistula-Oder offensive page). The counterpart is nazi-germany, the power the land came from; nazi-germany /ledger/68 records the same land as an occupation_end with counterpart second-polish-republic (no dossier), which eu-21 may retarget. The other German-held lands come by the January and March gains below, the Soviet-held Białystok and Przemyśl areas by the August gain.

region.text: the Reichsgau Wartheland: Greater Poland and Łódź, approximate (the region of nazi-germany /ledger/71)

ledger.note: 1945: Wartheland passes from Germany to Poland. "the 8th Guards Army reached Łódź by 18 January, and took it by 19 January"; Poznań was encircled by 25 January and the fighting in the city began on the 26th (Vistula-Oder offensive); the page gives no date for Poznań's fall, whose garrison held longer, and does not say that a Polish administration took the land over: the handover to the Polish state is the researcher's reading, mirroring nazi-germany /ledger/71 (confidence 2).

region.text: East Upper Silesia, the Katowice district, approximate, with the German Upper Silesia of Gliwice, Zabrze and Bytom that the gazetteer's Upper Silesia also holds; trimmed to the 1953 outline (nazi-germany /ledger/72 gives the untrimmed region, which runs 26 cells into Czech Silesia)

ledger.note: 1945: the Katowice district passes to Poland. On the night of 27 January Konev "secured the area undamaged" (Vistula-Oder offensive page, which dates the capture, not a Polish takeover): the handover is the researcher's reading, mirroring nazi-germany /ledger/72 (there confidence 3 for the capture). The region overlaps the Opole voivodeship of the August gain by about 41 cells, all in 1945.

region.text: the Ciechanów (Zichenau) district, a radius, approximate (the region of nazi-germany /ledger/73)

ledger.note: 1945: the Ciechanów district, annexed to East Prussia in 1939, passes to Poland. The East Prussian offensive page says only that it "lasted from 13 January to 25 April 1945" and that "Rokossovsky attacked across the Narew on 14 January"; neither it nor the Vistula-Oder offensive page names Ciechanów or Zichenau, so the month is a bridge over a silence, as in nazi-germany /ledger/73.

region.text: the former Free City of Danzig (the region of nazi-germany /ledger/77)

ledger.note: 1945: Danzig passes to Poland. "Danzig finally fell on 30 March 1945" (East Pomeranian offensive page, which says nothing of Polish authorities); the Oder-Neisse line page lists "the former Free City of Danzig" among the lands ceded to Poland and quotes Byrnes that "the assignment of this territory to Poland by Russia for administrative purposes had taken place before the Potsdam meeting". The date is the Soviet capture, the handover the researcher's reading (mirroring nazi-germany /ledger/77, confidence 3 for the capture).

region.text: the Reichsgau Danzig-West Prussia and German Farther Pomerania east of Szczecin: the Kuyavian-Pomeranian and Pomeranian voivodeships (Gdańsk, Gdynia, Bydgoszcz, Toruń, and Słupsk, Lębork and Bytów), approximate (the region of nazi-germany /ledger/78)

ledger.note: 1945: Danzig-West Prussia passes to Poland. The East Pomeranian offensive page gives "10 February - 4 April 1945" (introduction) and "24 February - 4 April 1945" (infobox), "Elbing finally fell on 10 March", "Gdingen was taken on 26 March 1945"; it does not mention Bydgoszcz, Toruń or Słupsk, so the month is the offensive's close and the south may have gone earlier. The handover is the researcher's reading, mirroring nazi-germany /ledger/78 (confidence 2). The Pomeranian voivodeship includes the German districts of Słupsk, Lębork and Bytów that the Oder-Neisse line page puts in the ceded "more than half of Pomerania".

region.text: the German territories east of the Oder–Neisse line that were not yet Polish in August: Lower Silesia, Opole Silesia, the Neumark (Lubusz), Farther Pomerania with Stettin (Szczecin) and southern East Prussia (the region of allied-occupied-germany /ledger/6); Danzig, the Pomeranian voivodeship and Upper Silesia (Gliwice, Bytom, Zabrze) are already Polish by the January and March gains above

ledger.note: 1945: the remaining German lands east of the Oder-Neisse line pass under Polish control by the Potsdam Agreement (Danzig, Pomerania west and north of the Vistula and German Upper Silesia are in the January and March gains from nazi-germany above; the gazetteer shows the five voivodeships plus those gains cover all but 12 border cells of the 1953 outline's 465 cells that lay outside pre-war Poland). "Finally on 2 August 1945, the Potsdam Agreement ... placed the German territories east of the Oder-Neisse line formally under Polish administrative control"; the Territorial changes page gives "some 101,000 square kilometres (39,000 square miles) in the west and north" and the Oder-Neisse page 112,000 km2 "in exchange for 187,000 km2 ... east of the Curzon Line". Szczecin was governed by a German communist-appointed mayor until 5 July 1945. Germany recognised the line in stages: the GDR in 1950, West Germany in 1970 (adhered 1972), united Germany in 1990. The Oder-Neisse line page: the line "placed almost all of Silesia, more than half of Pomerania" and "the former Free City of Danzig and the southern two-thirds of East Prussia" in Poland, and Soviet forces "expelled Polish administrators who tried to take Stettin in May and June 1945".

region.text: the part of the 1939 Soviet gain that lies inside modern Poland: the Białystok area and the Przemyśl area (the region of union-of-soviet-socialist-republics /ledger/50)

ledger.note: 1945, August: the Soviet Union returns the Białystok area to Poland. "On August 16, 1945, a border agreement between Poland and the USSR was signed"; "The Belastok Region was divided into Soviet Brest Region, Grodno Region and Polish Białystok Voivodeship" (Territorial changes of Poland page). The page names the Białystok region only; the Przemyśl area and the exact region are shape arithmetic copied from the USSR dossier, as in the corrected 1945 keyframe that removes Poland. The two ledgers now agree: Poland does not hold this land before August.
1949: the seat of government moves from Łódź to Warsaw. Infobox "Łódź (1947-1949) Warsaw (1949-1989)".

1952: the Republic of Poland becomes the Polish People's Republic under the July Constitution of 22 July 1952 (infobox "July Constitution: 22 July 1952"; the page says the state was called "Republic of Poland" only from 1947 to 1952). Same state, same colour (rule 2).

1989: the People's Republic ends and the Third Polish Republic begins. "The Parliament amended the Constitution on 29 December 1989"; infobox "Disestablished: 29 December 1989". Same state, same colour.

certainty.note: The western frontier is the Oder-Neisse river line, fixed in outline by Potsdam on 2 August 1945 but recognised only by the GDR in 1950 and West Germany in 1970-72; the eastern frontier is the Curzon-line agreement of 16 August 1945. Drawn sharp because both are survey or river lines, with the caveat that Poland held the western lands "under administration" until the 1990 treaty.
The German-Polish Border Treaty (signed 14 November 1990, in force 16 January 1992) and the 18 May 1992 confirmation with Ukraine settled every frontier.

notes: Five pages (budget up to 5; the Oder-Neisse page was also opened for the GDR dossier). Shared Wikidata: Cliopatria's "Kingdom of Poland" (kingdom-of-poland) and this row share Q36, but they are different states 600-plus years apart (the medieval and early modern Kingdom, and the post-1945 republic): two dossiers. The row starts in 1953 though the state began in 1945; Cliopatria has no Polish shape for 1940-1952, and the start taken here (1 January 1945, the Provisional Government of the Republic of Poland, as the Polish People's Republic page dates it; the review of 2026-11-01 moved it from June 1945) is the researcher's choice among the pages' 1944 (PKWN), 1945 (PGNU, June) and 1947 (infobox "Established") dates; the eu-22-x additions batch may write a wartime or Lublin dossier. The 1951 Polish-Soviet exchange of territory (Ustrzyki Dolne against the Sokal area) is dated in no opened page: Territorial changes of Poland and Poland-Ukraine border are silent, and the Polish People's Republic page is silent too, so no event or keyframe applies it. Czechoslovak border corrections (the Trstena agreement of 20 May 1945, later Klodzko, Glubczyce and Raciborz questions) are cut off or silent in the pages opened. Shape changes 1969 (+44 km2), 1990 (-467 km2) and 1992 (-43 km2) are outline noise or tiny sea-border adjustments; the 1990 and 1992 years match the border treaty (signed 1990, in force 1992). No ruler strip: the infobox lists of Bierut, Ochab, Gomulka, Gierek, Kania, Jaruzelski are unlabelled party and state offices, and the Third Republic page is silent on most presidents' dates. No wars listed: the pages opened record none for Poland after 1945 that moved a border; the spillover of the 2022 war (17 million Ukrainian refugees "crossing the border to Poland") moved no border. The Soviet Army stayed in Poland until 18 September 1993 ("The last post-Soviet troops left Poland on 18 September 1993"), by Warsaw Pact arrangement, not drawn as an occupation. Counterparts: second-polish-republic (no dossier existed on 2026-11-01; its Cliopatria row runs 1919-1939) and allied-occupied-germany (exists). The Allied-occupied-germany ledger carries the matching loss in 1945-08. Repair of 2026-11-01 (review eu-22-c): the formation now mirrors the neighbours' ledgers. Found 1945-01 on the General Government land with counterpart nazi-germany; gains from nazi-germany for Wartheland, the Katowice district and the Ciechanów district (1945-01) and for Danzig and Danzig-West Prussia (1945-03), the regions of nazi-germany /ledger/71-73, 77, 78 (the Upper Silesia region trimmed to the 1953 outline); the Potsdam gain from allied-occupied-germany (1945-08) keeps the five voivodeships of allied-occupied-germany /ledger/6; a new gain from the USSR (1945-08) mirrors union-of-soviet-socialist-republics /ledger/50. Checked with the gazetteer: of the 465 cells of the 1953 outline that lie outside the Second Republic of 1939, the five voivodeships and the nazi-germany gains cover 453; the 12 left are border slivers on the Oder and the Carpathians, outline noise. Three more pages were opened for the repair (Vistula-Oder, East Pomeranian and East Prussian offensives), so eight in all against a budget of five. Disagreement with the review: the reviewer's wider August region (1953 outline minus the Second Republic) was not adopted, because Danzig, the Pomeranian voivodeship and Upper Silesia are already gained from nazi-germany in January and March and the gazetteer shows the five voivodeships plus those gains complete the outline.
